entries.title: Iran War Threatens the Economies of Trump's Gulf Allies
entries.summary: The freshly renewed conflict continues to stymie efforts by Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the U.A.E. to expand their non-oil revenue and global reach.
entries.content:
The U.S. and Iran have resumed military strikes — trapping America’s partners in the Middle East in volatility that could hurt their economies for years to come.

U.S. Central Command on Sunday launched the first American strikes on Iranian forces in more than a month, saying the targets posed “an imminent threat” to civilian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran launched retaliatory missiles at American forces in Jordan hours later. The renewed violence came after the Trump administration had argued it was weakening Iran’s grip on the strait and bolstering energy shipments through the crucial waterway by deploying U.S. naval forces. The administration has also applied unprecedented sanction pressure on the country, which led analysts to predict Iran would retaliate. Now, experts believe that the potential for tit-for-tat strikes will continue even if all-out conflict is avoided.

“Both sides are now settling in for a long U.S.-Iran war,” Richard Fontaine of the Center for a New American Security think tank wrote on X. “The best bet now is on a protracted economic contest, enforced largely but not exclusively through military means.”

American allies in the region have sold themselves in recent years as reliable, safe and business-minded nations. But the U.S.-Iran war has challenged that narrative as those same allies have faced Iranian attacks on U.S. bases they host, arrangements once seen as a measure of security against such attacks, as well as their own infrastructure.

The new strikes are, for countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, “a continuation of a risky stalemate,” Anna Jacobs Khalaf, a fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute think tank, told NOTUS. “Gulf states are under no illusions anymore about their influence with Trump. They will always try and lobby for de-escalation … [but the] bottom line is that there is very little trust left in this U.S. administration.”

That stalemate threatens those countries’ efforts to attract outside investment and to develop significant revenue streams beyond exporting fossil fuels. Semafor reported Sunday that plans for three Saudi companies to raise money through initial public offerings have been shelved, signaling shrinking expectations of attracting foreign money. The opening of a multibillion-dollar branch of the Wynn Resorts empire in the U.A.E. has been postponed, and hiring there has seen its sharpest drop since the early months of the pandemic. And Qatar has cut funding for government departments and aid.

Several major events in the Gulf countries, including multiple F1 races and conferences, were postponed in the early weeks of the war. While other high-profile gatherings that are expected to draw thousands of attendees, like Qatar’s Doha Forum and a crypto conference in Dubai, remain on the calendar, those planning to attend the events said they regularly discuss possible delays or disruptions.

Middle Eastern policymakers, particularly those from nations with deep pockets, had expected geopolitical matters like long-standing, unresolved U.S.-Iran animosity would be secondary to economics for Trump.

“The big failed bet from all these Gulf states was they bet the Trump administration cared more about making money … Ultimately, Trump reached a place where he cares more about not conceding a loss to Iran than he cares about the entire economy of the region going down the tube,” said Andrew Leber, a professor at Tulane University.

A White House official said in an email that Trump has “extraordinary relationships with all of our Gulf partners.”

“President Trump has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy. Unfortunately, Iran chose the path of violence by killing American troops, committing international acts of terrorism, and lashing out at its neighbors in the region — and the Commander-in-Chief ensures that they reap the consequences,” the official continued.

Regional governments and royal families are simultaneously entangled in Trump’s personal financial interests and his promises of delivering prosperity for Americans. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund put $2 billion into a private-equity fund run by Trump’s son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner, a firm in which Qatar and the U.A.E. have also invested hundreds of millions of dollars. World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency business driven by the families of Trump and his adviser Steve Witkoff, is preparing to launch a bank whose largest stake belongs to Emirati royal Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al Nahyan. Meanwhile, Trump has claimed he has secured over $2 trillion in Gulf investments for America.

“The thing about investing this money is: You can give the money and hope … but you have to be willing to cut off the money or otherwise impose costs if they don't do what you want,” Leber said, noting no Arab state has threatened Trump with withdrawing any of those investments.

Though already wealthy, those countries want to ensure they remain so, by preserving the social contracts that allow autocratic families to rule and avoiding instability.

“Gulf leaders expected those enormous commitments to deliver security, access and strategic predictability,” Abdullah Baabood, a scholar of international relations at Waseda University in Japan, told NOTUS. But instead, the war is “damaging precisely the sectors their diversification strategies depend on: tourism, aviation, logistics, investment and non-oil industries,” he wrote in a text message.

Leber noted that big investments by international companies in sectors the Gulf states focused on, such as data centers, have not been announced this year, in contrast to 2025.

“I don’t think people who have invested time and money in these countries are going to bolt. It’s just harder to attract the next generation of firms and investments to the region,” Leber said.

The entertainment and tourism sectors are among those most directly stymied by the ongoing conflict, he noted. Though their direct contributions to national economies are smaller than those of other sectors, countries like Saudi Arabia had hoped growth in those areas would soften their global reputation and counter long-standing perceptions that they are too conservative for foreigners’ comfort.

“There’s a strong effort to try to go against the image that we cannot host any events,” said Aziz Alghashian, a fellow at the Gulf International Forum. “The Saudis and others, they're far more wary of image and perception than before … they will have to work a lot harder in showing there is more investment and there’s room for investment.”

Baabood argued that “governments can continue building hotels, resorts and venues, but they cannot easily compensate for weaker international demand.”

Riyadh previously addressed unexpected regional flare-ups like the war in Gaza from 2023 onward by emphasizing its agility and ability to quickly shift its plans, Alghashian said. And Leber noted Gulf governments generally have preserved enough reserves of capital to sustain them through “a year or two of turbulent times.”

Still, both analysts highlighted long-term concerns. The Iran war has sapped decision-makers’ time and energy and interrupted their planning, Alghashian said — and driven a rethink that could leave the U.S. less influential in the region.

Even as the Trump administration argues it’s isolating Tehran economically, Gulf states may soon base their planning more on fellow countries in the region — including Iran — than the U.S.

“Accommodation with Iran is increasingly not just a foreign-policy preference,” Baabood said. “It’s an economic-security necessity.”

entries.title: Mamdani's Next Battleground? Berlin.
entries.summary: Staffers from Germany’s Die Linke party travelled to New York last year to learn from the DSA’s campaign as they try to win a mayor’s race in Berlin.
entries.content:
BERLIN — A mayor's race. A Muslim candidate from the left. A promise to make one of the world's great cities affordable again.

Sound familiar? This time it’s not New York. It's Berlin, where Elif Eralp, Die Linke's candidate, is running to become the city's first Muslim mayor, as well as the first Left Party mayor since the city’s reunification. Recent polling shows her leading with 20.7% of the vote against the Christian Democratic Union of Germany Party and the Alternative for Germany party, which are polling around 18.9% and 17.6%, respectively.

The Sept. 20 election echoes the race that gripped America last year, when political newcomer Zohran Mamdani toppled former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic primary and rewrote the rules of what a mayoral campaign could look like.

In several interviews, Die Linke’s party members have made clear they drew inspiration from Mamdani’s successful mayoral campaign, first from afar and then much closer to New York’s City Hall. Party co-chair Ines Schwerdtner traveled to New York with other party officials to watch the Mamdani operation up close.

Schwerdtner went last fall to learn more about efforts by the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as New York’s progressive Working Families Party, to expand their bases of support in the city and the U.S. more broadly.

“We embrace Mamdani's victory,” said Janis Ehling, the Die Linke federal managing director, which is the equivalent of an executive director for a party in the U.S. “We learned a lot [from] them, especially when it comes to community organizing, door-knocking, canvassing campaigns.”

“I think we're going in the same direction,” Ehling told NOTUS.

A far-left candidate breaking through in Germany’s capital city would stand in contrast to what’s happening in the state government, where the far right appears to be surging.

“It would be really significant for German politics as a whole when you think of [World War II history],” said Thorsten Holzhauser, a historian and political scientist in Germany.

“They have tried to play down identity politics and parts of their agenda,” he said of Die Linke, “and highlight the more economic and social issues such as housing, such as cost of living, things that are important to middle-class voters and working-class voters at the same time.”

The Left Party's Berlin Election Campaign with Lead Candidate Eralp 26234672086988 (3419x2279, AR: 1.50)
While elections operate completely differently in Germany than in the United States — voters cast ballots for the party rather than the candidate — Die Linke has selected Eralp to represent them in the election.

“We have the chance to have a Left mayor in Berlin, and that's a huge chance,” Ehling said. “In Germany, the far right is rising too, and that would be a big symbol of hope for all over Germany, like Mamdani was in the United States.”

Grace Mausser, co-chair of New York City's DSA chapter, told NOTUS that she sees similarities in the United States’ and Germany’s partisan politics.

“I think it's critical that we not only inspire each other and give each other encouragement as we're working in sometimes dangerous conditions, yeah, but also that our work compounds each other and doesn't take away from what each is doing,” she said.

The comparison is one that the Die Linke party officials have leaned into publicly. When Mamdani won in November, the party's Berlin branch posted on X, translated into English, “Whether New York or Berlin: We all want affordable rents and a good life for our families and friends!” Eralp said in interviews that she sees Mamdani’s win as an example for left candidates.

Part of the Die Linke party’s appeal in Berlin is Eralp's pledge to force corporations to own fewer apartments to help lower housing costs. She's paired that with a push for rent caps on public housing, a new city office for tenant protection and a discounted transit pass, a platform that is gaining traction in the city that’s faced an affordability crisis.

Beyond Eralp’s affordability proposals, Mausser said, her immigrant background also resonates with voters.

“One thing I found interesting in the Berlin mayoral election specifically is the potential to activate and politicize an immigrant population within the city,” Mausser told NOTUS. “We saw that with Zohran activating and politicizing a Muslim and Southeast Asian voter base, and I think Elif has the potential to do that with the Turkish voter base in Berlin.”

She added: “That to me is so important because the right wing explicitly doesn't want people who are not coded as a native to their home country to be able to vote, to have a political voice. So a figure like Zohran, a figure like Elif, a figure like [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez], who is obviously Hispanic and will speak to that population, them running proudly as non-white people in majority white countries, I think it sends an important signal on who belongs in each of those places.”

Holzhauser, the political scientist, sought to temper expectations of what a Die Linke victory could yield, saying that Germany’s coalition system of governing will make it nearly impossible to enact Eralp’s and Die Linke’s proposed policies.

“It will be very difficult for Die Linke to realize and to bring forward their agenda in such a coalition,” he said. “Especially when it comes to housing, when it comes to the very controversial issue of expropriating major players in the housing sector, which is a very important issue for Die Linke, but which has been opposed by every other party and especially by the potential partners.”

entries.title: Trump’s Drug Enforcement Leader Violates a Financial Law
entries.summary: Terry Cole was months late disclosing stock purchases worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.
entries.content:
Drug Enforcement Administration Administrator Terry Cole violated a federal financial disclosure law by failing to properly disclose hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of personal stock purchases, according to a NOTUS review of new federal records.

Cole was between four and five months late revealing December 2025 purchases of Tesla, Nike and Super Micro Computer stock that, taken together, is worth between $300,000 and $750,000, a filing with the independent Office of Government Ethics indicates.

Federal law requires high-ranking executive branch officials to publicly disclose individual stock trades within 45 days of making them. The government requires such disclosure to defend against insider trading, to curb conflicts of interest and to enhance transparency.

In a statement to NOTUS, the DEA said Cole requested on June 29 that the agency waive any fee for his late disclosure — penalties begin at $200 — and agency ethics officials granted that request.

“Administrator Cole had been in his position for only six months when he conducted these transactions,” the DEA said in its statement. “DEA’s ethics officials identified no conflicts.”

The DEA did not address other questions, including why Cole purchased the stocks and why he waited past a federal deadline to disclose them.

Office of Government Ethics spokesperson Patrick Shepherd declined to comment, noting his agency “does not respond to questions about specific individuals.”

Super Micro Computer stock has increased in value since Cole purchased his shares in December, while Nike and Tesla stock have declined in value.

Tesla, Nike and Super Micro Computer do not appear to do business with the DEA.

In a federal ethics agreement Cole signed in March 2025, prior to his Senate confirmation, he agreed to divest of stock he held in Amazon.com — a contractor for the Department of Justice, of which the DEA is a part — and “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest” while leading the DEA.

Cole, who leads an agency of more than 10,000 people tasked with fighting drug traffickers and criminal syndicates, has served in law enforcement for more than three decades, including much of that time at the DEA. From 2023 to 2025, he served as Virginia's secretary of public safety and homeland security.

In addition to his current DEA position, which he assumed in July 2025 after a 50-47 Senate confirmation vote, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi tapped Cole in August 2025 to lead Washington, D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Force. Cole’s appointment unraveled in a matter of days amid a legal fight over whether the Trump administration could effectively seize control of the city’s police department.

In addition to Cole, several top Trump administration officials have made notable personal financial trades or deals during recent months.

They include FBI Director Kash Patel, Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, Ambassador to Italy Tilman Fertitta, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, Federal Highway Administration Administrator Sean McMaster, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler, former U.S. Agency for Global Media leader Kari Lake, Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal, Department of Homeland Security Undersecretary Pedro Allende, Environmental Protection Agency Assistant Administrator Douglas Troutman and former Department of Health and Human Services general counsel Mike Stuart.

Trump himself has been the subject of significant scrutiny regarding the intersection of his personal finances and public service. The president has reported thousands of stock and bond trades during the past year and has routinely engaged in private crypto and other business ventures since returning to the White House in 2025.

Congress is actively considering banning federal lawmakers — but not yet executive branch officials — from buying individual stocks in the first place.

entries.title: The Road to RFK
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Sept. 1, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

A new Commanders stadium is coming, that much we know. But no one can agree on how anybody will get there.

At an open house hosted by Metro last week, some Ward 7 residents clashed with officials who’ve said building a second rail station is an impossibility at the old RFK site where a new stadium is being built, NOTUS’ Zara Norman reports.

“It's just not feasible, and it's not just about numbers,” Randy Clarke, the general manager of WMATA, told NOTUS. “It’d be this big station in the sky, on a curb no one could get to, and it doesn't actually help with capacity. … There's just no there there.”

Metro estimates it would cost $1 billion to build a second station, and it wouldn’t even be ready in time for the team’s projected move in 2030. A new rapid-transit bus line — dubbed “the Gold Line” — as well as improvements at the Stadium-Armory Metro station will do the trick, Clarke said. Not everyone is convinced.

“I don't really trust the numbers and the evaluation they did,” Ward 6 council member Charles Allen told NOTUS. “The option to build that new station has got to remain on the table, because it really is about if we want to see this as a growth opportunity in this part of the city or not.”

For residents, part of the skepticism stems from the failure of D.C.’s streetcar, which ran into trouble along the exact H Street corridor Metro is proposing for the Gold Line.

“The RFK campus needs a durable transit solution if the city is going to see a return on its billion-dollar investment,” Hill East resident David Wyman told NOTUS. “The streetcar hasn't worked. Metro stations are forever.”

When the political winds change in January, it’s possible that new leadership might revisit adding a second station. Though a spokesperson for Janeese Lewis George declined to give her thoughts on transit options supplying the area, Allen told NOTUS he has a “hunch” that “she’ll at least be much more open-minded.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Construction on the controversial White House ballroom can continue, per a 5-4 ruling that came down Monday afternoon from the Supreme Court, NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports. A majority of the justices ruled that historic preservationists lacked standing to sue.

A D.C. police officer died Monday morning after sustaining a gunshot wound inside the Second District police station in Northwest, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports. City officials say there was no indication that anyone else was involved, but did not share further details on what occurred. This is the second line-of-duty death for the Metropolitan Police Department this year, and one of only seven that have taken place since 2000.

Chronic understaffing at D.C.’s Department of Behavioral Health means the city’s suicide and crisis lifeline, 988, has one of the nation’s lowest pickup rates, City Cast D.C. reports.

A historic D.C. building near the White House, Hamilton Square, sold for $126 million at a steep loss: The seller acquired it for $198 million in 2012, the Washington Business Journal reports.

Rush, the U Street gay club seized by U.S. marshals last month, was plagued by problems from conception to launch and finally to eviction, City Cast D.C. reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Ready for takeoff. Washington Manassas Airport is now certified for commercial passenger flights, WJLA reports. The airport, which will launch its commercial service next year, might benefit from rising enplanement costs at Dulles, the Washington Business Journal reports.





FROM YOUR FEED


Soon after President Donald Trump announced he would change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, many locals, including NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle, began noodling on the implications for the District. PoPville reports that someone took matters into their own hands Monday, plastering “America” over a street sign for Ontario Place Northwest.

https://x.com/PoPville/status/2094418845050015815?s=20



SPORTS

High school football season has arrived and we are on the lookout for the DMV’s top talents. NOTUS’ Noah Ferguson will be covering all the action across the District and its suburbs this fall, highlighting what makes this area one of the country’s most respected high school sports hotbeds.

Each week, Noah will highlight five local football players who stood out over the weekend. Our very first group includes a freshman from Bullis who rushed for more than 150 yards and an Oakton senior who turned heads with a 99-yard touchdown run.

Mystics Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen were called up to Team USA on Monday ahead of the FIBA World Cup. NOTUS’ Alex Schiffer reports that Washington’s young duo will replace Kelsey Plum and A’Ja Wilson, who stepped back because of injury concerns. The international tournament runs Friday to Sept. 13 in Berlin.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Braves, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) Ulysses S. Grant. He was arrested for speeding in a horse-drawn carriage in 1872. A special shout-out to Willie Wynn, who answered first.

entries.title: Data Center Chaos
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump tries to settle the data center debate. What to watch for in the Massachusetts primaries. Copying Zohran in Berlin. Army secretary resigns. And: It’s hard to make economic plans with the Iran war going on next door.





THE LATEST

Chaos season is officially declared. Welcome to September of an election year, the traditional start of campaigns locking in messages and getting serious about executing them. The hot primary summer now turns into a brisk messaging fall.

Republicans, running against historical headwinds and alongside a president with the second-term blues, have said all year to ignore the polls and wait for the fall. The money bombs will drop, the midterm convention will focus candidates on their general election goals.

However, if this first Real Week of Getting Serious is any indication, it’s going to be a very chaotic fall for the GOP. Party leaders and candidates have spent the last few weeks carefully constructing a new narrative around data centers, one that reflects widespread voter skepticism toward the projects. But with one Truth Social post yesterday, Donald Trump screwed that all up. “Let Data Reign,” he wrote, calling all opponents of data center construction idiots, basically.

Uh, no we’re not, some Republicans quickly responded. “President Trump and I don’t see eye to eye on this issue,” Darren Bailey, the Republican nominee for governor in Illinois, posted on X. The party has been working hard to embrace the gray areas in the data center debate, to show that it is listening. The president just snapped things back to black and white. That’s not message discipline.

“He just put every Republican’s name on the deed to every data center in America, and on the return address to every power bill,” Democratic strategist Jesse Ferguson, who has thought a lot about the politics of this issue, told us.

Ironically, the data center industry itself is trying to be more attentive to that gray-area thinking than the president is. NOTUS’ Mara Hoplamazian reports on how data center developers are actively wooing communities nowadays — not only with promises of riches but, in the case of one project in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, a vow to deposit $10,000 in the account of every family living there. Some locals have called it a bribe, Mara reports. Jury’s out on whether these sweetened deals are good politics.

Open tabs: JD Vance Calls El-Sayed ‘Very, Very Evil’ (NOTUS); Top General Says Military Has ‘No Plans’ to Deploy to Polls During Midterms (NOTUS); Laura Loomer faces fresh criticism over racist comments (Reuters); Republicans Are Urging SCOTUS to Give Them a Discount on TV Ads (NOTUS)





From Massachusetts


Old dogs have their day? Tonight’s primary elections in Massachusetts could serve as a real narrative-buster in the Democratic conversation about age. Eighty-year-old Sen. Ed Markey is cruising in the Democratic senate primary polls against 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton. The younger candidate has tried to make age an issue, but that has not made a discernible polling dent (if you believe polls). Markey, of course, also beat a much younger guy in his last primary. In both cases, reporters pointed out that Markey had been in office longer than his opponent had been alive. In 2020, voters didn’t care. Will they this time?

Down the ballot, there is another chance for the age-as-liability truism to go poof. NOTUS’ Kate Nocera reported recently on the Democratic primary in the 1st Congressional District, where Rep. Richard Neal, 77, says he’s got nothing to worry about from challenger Jeromie Whalen, 39.

But don’t discount the narrative just yet: In the 8th District, observers say 71-year-old Rep. Stephen Lynch is in a tight Democratic primary battle with 39-year-old challenger Patrick Roath, who says the incumbent is too old and too moderate for the Boston-area district.

From Germany


Zohran Mamdani is big in Berlin. NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz reports from Berlin on a concerted — and welcomed — effort by Germany’s Die Linke party to copy Mamdani’s success in New York for the Sept. 20 mayoral election in Berlin. Die Linke is hoping voters elect Elif Eralp, who would be the first Muslim mayor of the city and first leftist since the Berlin Wall fell. “We learned a lot [from Mamdani], especially when it comes to community organizing, door-knocking, canvassing campaigns,” Die Linke’s equivalent of an executive director, Janis Ehling, told Daniella.  

From the Pentagon


An Army, less one: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll “spoke to the president about the current state of the Army and submitted his resignation” yesterday, an Army official told NOTUS’ Joe Gould, capping off a tension-filled tenure between Driscoll and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll had butted heads with Hegseth over the direction of the Army and the secretary’s removal of senior officers — on top of the strain between the two men after Hegseth forced Gen. Randy George, the Army’s chief of staff, to retire in April.

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Sports desk: DMV High School Football Players of the Week, by Noah Ferguson





NEW ON NOTUS

With friends like these: The ongoing war with Iran is stifling efforts by some U.S. allies in the Middle East to plan their economic futures, NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed reports. Regional governments hoping to diversify their international positions beyond oil “can continue building hotels, resorts and venues, but they cannot easily compensate for weaker international demand,” Abdullah Baabood, a professor at Waseda University in Japan, told Akbar.

entries.title: Want an Animal Shelter? A Lazy River? Cash? Data Centers Want to Know.
entries.summary: How data center developers are spending their way into communities.
entries.content:
In a few years, the city of Saline, Michigan, will have renovated its recreation center’s locker rooms, tiled the pool deck, expanded the children's play area, installed a waterfall and constructed a lazy river. Down the road, part of OpenAI’s Project Stargate, a 2.2 million-square-foot, $43 billion data center, will hum away, churning out the next generation of artificial intelligence.

As public sentiment on data centers has soured, AI companies are leveling up their efforts to sweeten the deal for communities that host them. In Saline, that included a $10 million donation from OpenAI, Oracle and other companies for a new and improved recreation center.

In Richland Parish, Louisiana, teachers got $50,000 bonuses from Meta. Compass Datacenters forked over $15 million for a new animal shelter in Ellis County, Texas. In Florida, developers for the failed Project Tango offered to hide their building from view with a small forest of pines, palms and native shrubs. NorthPoint Development has proposed giving $10,000 to every household in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, if it’s allowed to build a massive data center for Amazon — a dangling carrot some residents have characterized as a bribe.

Politicians from both parties are pushing the deal sweeteners too. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore’s energy office told counties to make “wish lists” for data center developers, and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is pitching free electricity for towns willing to play host.

This summer’s data center backlash has underlined a glaring lack of guidance from federal and state leaders on what tech companies owe the communities they’re building in; in Washington, a growing slate of proposals range from requiring developers to procure and pay for their own power, and taxing data centers to prepare for potential AI-related job losses.

In the absence of comprehensive federal regulation, local officials are largely left to negotiate agreements with data center developers themselves. For many of the towns being targeted by developers, the scale of wealth AI companies can bring to the table could be transformative. The benefits they promise, though, rely on the success of a nascent industry that’s been met with fear and doubt. And as developers try to fight widespread distrust and opposition, even multimillion-dollar donations don’t seem to be moving public opinion.

In Michigan, Saline Township’s leadership had voted last year to block the data center development. The developer sued over the zoning decision soon after. The township settled, with officials negotiating several community benefits: a few million dollars for emergency services, farmland preservation and other community investments.

The recreation center revamp came up more casually, said Saline Mayor Brian Marl.

Once it was clear the data center would be built, Marl organized a lunch with Oracle and the other developers. He gave them a tour of the recreation center, and told them about all the work the city hoped to do on the building. Then, the Friday before the groundbreaking, he got a call at 8 p.m. — the companies wanted to give the city $10 million dollars to help with that project.

Marl says the move was an obvious attempt by the companies to ingratiate themselves in the Saline community. But it’s not clear that $10 million went very far toward that goal. Marl is still fielding calls and taking meetings with residents who are fervently trying to stop the project, even as construction moves forward.

“I don’t think it’s game-changing locally, in terms of people’s feelings toward this specific data center, or data center developments more broadly,” he said.

Some offers from developers have backfired.

In Osage County, Oklahoma, Google’s efforts to win support for a data center were thwarted when a local volunteer fire department rejected a $250,000 donation — a sum larger than the department’s annual budget — because of the community’s concerns. That project is the subject of three separate lawsuits, one involving attacks over a lack of government transparency.

City officials in Sand Springs, which annexed the land that would be used for the data center, have negotiated tax agreements and other contributions from Google for community projects. But Osage County Commissioner Steve Talburt hasn’t been impressed.

He’s refused to sign nondisclosure agreements related to the project, despite pressure from Google. The company offered the county a few hundred thousand dollars per year as a payment in lieu of taxes, Talburt said. When he and the other commissioners pushed back, the company cut the county out of the tax agreement completely.

A few weeks ago, a contractor for Google came to visit him, asking what the company could do to smooth things over. The contractor offered to put up extra money for county schools or infrastructure, Talburt said. He declined.

“Google’s just trying to throw money around to get everybody on board, and that’s not good enough,” he said. “It’s not going to make it right. And Osage County is not going to sell out.”

Many negotiations have revolved around similar informal donations or contributions from data center developers. Those aren’t always legally enforceable, said Daniel Metzger, a legal expert with Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law.

Anti-bribery laws make it difficult for local governments to accept benefits explicitly in exchange for approving projects. Local officials can create binding agreements for benefits that are connected to the potential harms a project may cause, regulating water and electricity use, or forcing companies to pay to improve the emergency services they may rely on.

In one of the first formal benefit agreements for a data center in the U.S., the city of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, cut a deal with developers that requires them to use only clean energy, hire locally, make yearly reports and pay $20 million dollars into community development funds.

Agreements like those are filling a gap where coordinated federal or state legislation is absent, Metzger said, especially agreements that include transparency requirements around water and energy use.

The benefit agreements can be so lucrative that some state and local officials are banking on AI companies to fund their most pie-in-the-sky ambitions. St. Louis officials got a developer to pay roughly $15 million toward public Wi-Fi across the city, among other projects. In West Virginia, where Nvidia and Microsoft are building what could be the largest data center on earth, the state’s 20-year plan published last month aims to eliminate state income tax and boost funding for local schools by attracting massive hyperscale projects.

Still, evidence that community benefit agreements lead to better situations — especially in smaller towns — is mixed, said Devashree Saha, director of the U.S. Clean Energy Economy Program at the World Resources Institute.

“Typically it’s not an even playing field between communities and developers,” she said. “It becomes difficult for community coalitions to hold the developer accountable.”

If a company goes bankrupt or sells a development to another entity and those benefits dry up, it can leave a community that was banking on financial support scrambling, Saha said.

Even without formal agreements or massive donations, a new data center can fundamentally change a place.

In Ellendale, North Dakota, a data center development has more than tripled the town’s tax base. Mayor Don Flaherty says in the next three years, it’s projected to grow from $3.5 million to $37 million.

The data center has touched seemingly every part of life in Ellendale — for better and for worse, Flaherty says. Heavy trucks have torn up the roads. This summer, about 2,600 workers are in town to construct the buildings — more than doubling the town’s population of 1,100. Flaherty says it’s been fun to meet new people, though concerns about crime and traffic have increased.

Hundreds of jobs for locals in Ellendale are on the horizon. The full-time population could grow by up to 600. With all the new tax revenue, the town is planning to upgrade the senior center and ambulance hall, refresh the downtown and work on a walking trail. Down the road, Flaherty is eyeing a new fire department building and a law enforcement center.

Meanwhile, residents are saving money on energy bills as their utility company sells more power to the data center and its profits increase, South Dakota Searchlight reported. Applied Digital, the company behind the development, is helping to finance new housing.

But rent has in some cases doubled, pushing families out of town. And there’s a constant hum at the edge of town.

Flaherty didn’t do any formal negotiation with Applied Digital — which he acknowledges could have been naive. He says he has some concern about a data center bubble bursting, leaving Ellendale behind. Mostly, though, he’s seeing the benefits.

“This is what I believe is the answer for rural America, and it doesn’t necessarily have to be data centers, but some type of project of this nature that can stimulate your economy,” he said. “I guess those are the things that outweigh the worries.”

entries.title: A New Commanders Stadium Is Coming. How Will Anybody Get There?
entries.summary: The question of whether to build a second train station at RFK has divided a neighborhood — and city government.
entries.content:
There’s a lot we know about the forthcoming Commanders stadium at RFK. Plans say it will have 65,000 seats, be accompanied by 6,600 new homes and generate $4 billion in tax revenue.

One thing we don’t yet know: how fans will get there.

Local leaders expect a significant number of the estimated 65,000 fans coming to games to use public transit, but Metro (and outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser) has already ruled out building a new rail station. The transit agency says a new station would likely cost over $1 billion, wouldn’t meaningfully expand rail capacity and wouldn’t even be completed in time for the stadium’s 2030 opening.

“It's just not feasible, and it's not just about numbers,” Randy Clarke, the general manager of WMATA, told NOTUS. “It'd be this big station in the sky, on a curb no one could get to, and it doesn't actually help with capacity. …There's just no there there.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Instead, the agency wants to expand the existing Stadium-Armory station and roll out a new rapid transit bus line, dubbed “the Gold Line,” that would run along H Street and Benning Road Northeast, stretching from Union Station to the RFK campus and eventually beyond.

Not everyone’s sold on the idea. Some Ward 7 residents and Ward 6 Council member Charles Allen — who chairs the D.C. Council’s transportation committee — say Metro didn’t sufficiently study whether a new station is feasible. Some residents don’t trust the agency’s reliance on an east-west road connection after the failure of D.C.’s streetcar along the exact same corridor.

“The RFK campus needs a durable transit solution if the city is going to see a return on its billion-dollar investment,” David Wyman, a Hill East resident, told NOTUS. “The streetcar hasn't worked. Metro stations are forever.”

At an open house held by Metro last week and intended as a way for Ward 7 residents to talk to city officials about transit options, John Capozzi grew increasingly frustrated. As he milled around the St. Coletta school gymnasium, he saw more and more material that treated the new station question as settled.

“I thought we were gonna talk about options,” said Capozzi, a Commanders fan who is active in local politics and has lived in Southeast D.C. for decades.

Both Metro and Bowser dismissed the idea of a second station “before it really even was an idea,” Council member Allen said. He believes they only studied one of the area’s most challenging build sites.

“I don't really trust the numbers and the evaluation they did,” Allen told NOTUS. “The option to build that new station has got to remain on the table, because it really is about if we want to see this as a growth opportunity in this part of the city or not.”

Metro maintains that an improved Stadium-Armony station — with an expanded entrance, more elevators and escalators — can handle the traffic, when combined with the Gold line.

Clarke said he understands that the city may have lost some trust with the streetcar’s failure, but Metro won’t repeat those mistakes with a rapid bus transit service.

“The real issue was [the streetcar] was put on the curb, and once it's on the curb, you're fighting with everyone else on the curb, and you can't really have priority,” Clarke told NOTUS. “[We want] exclusive lanes. We want it in the middle. We want single priority. We want 60-foot buses, offboard payment platforms. So, basically, it'll look and feel a lot like a light rail line.”

Allen doesn’t think the city should take an either-or approach, and that a second station is worth building even if it doesn’t happen in time for 2030. He pointed to the success of the NoMa neighborhood and its transit-oriented development.

“Transit helped make that happen. If we are saying we want to be in a growth mode for our city, we’ve got to invest in transit,” Allen said. “A station there is actually about a lot more than just the stadium — it’s about building out the neighborhood.”

It’s possible that the D.C. Council could revisit the conversation of a second station down the line, particularly with the political winds changing in January when three new Council members and a new mayor take office. A spokesperson for Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee for mayor, declined to comment on her position.

“I have a hunch she'll at least be much more open-minded,” Allen told NOTUS.

entries.title: DMV High School Football Players of the Week
entries.summary: An Eastern linebacker and a Bullis freshman are among the standouts from Week 1.
entries.content:
The high school football season has officially kicked off in the D.C. area, and a new crop of local talent has already begun to emerge. This past weekend marked the start of a new year for public programs in the city and in Northern Virginia. Many of the region’s private schools also played their first games. Next week, Maryland publics will join the party. Here are five players who stood out in Week 1:

Austin Barber, Senior, Wide Receiver, DeMatha

The Stags opened their Washington Catholic Athletic Conference title defense with a 35-14 statement win over Archbishop Spalding Friday, and Barber made his mark with two game-changing plays. The senior wide receiver first hauled in a 45-yard touchdown pass with a defender draped on his back, helping give DeMatha an early edge against the Cavaliers, four-time defending champs in the Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association. He later returned a punt 42 yards for his second score as the Stags pulled away for their 22nd-straight victory and first under interim head coach Bryce Bevill, who took over for longtime coach Bill McGregor this offseason.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Kevin Coates, Senior, Athlete, Alexandria City

Coates did it all for Alexandria City in a surprising 21-7 victory over Lake Braddock. The senior split time between quarterback and wide receiver on offense, racking up 126 all-purpose yards and catching a touchdown in the third quarter. On defense, he nabbed an interception as the Titans scored 21 unanswered points in the second half to notch their first victory over Lake Braddock since 2008.

Kyron Gaskins, Senior, Linebacker, Eastern

Gaskins shined in his first start as a Rambler after transferring from DeMatha this offseason. The senior was the anchor of a defense that manhandled New Town in a 29-6 Eastern victory. The Ramblers, who won the D.C. State Athletic Association AA crown for the first time ever last season, will look to contend for another city crown with sophomore quarterback Nijel Hubbard taking over for his brother, Jeremiah, under center.

Deylen Jones, Senior, Athlete, Oakton

The Cougars wasted little time flashing their offensive firepower in a 49-7 rout of Edison. Jones, a Harvard commit, put on a performance to remember. He totaled 221 all-purpose yards and scored three touchdowns, including a 99-yard touchdown run through the heart of the Eagles’ defense. The dominant performance marked the program’s first victory under new coach Said Aziz, who is looking to take the Vienna program to new heights in a loaded Concorde District.

Kyree Marshall, Freshman, Running Back, Bullis

Marshall burst onto the scene for the Bulldogs Saturday in his varsity debut. He gashed Bishop Ireton for 153 rushing yards and two touchdowns on just eight carries as Bullis earned a 49-14 victory. With Marshall in the backfield, coach Skyler Springs’ team scored more points than it did in any game last season.

entries.title: Whistleblower Says Secret USPS Plan May Endanger Millions of Mail-in Ballots
entries.summary: A new portal will “almost certainly have significant operating problems” due to rushed development, the whistleblower said.
entries.content:
An anonymous federal official warned in a whistleblower report released Tuesday that the U.S. Postal Service plans to secretly and unlawfully implement the Trump administration’s mail-in ballot restrictions through a “rushed” new system that could prevent voters from receiving their ballots.

The whistleblower said in a disclosure to Congress that the USPS began working on a new set of untested information technology systems, including the “Federal Ballot Mail Portal,” in June 2026 despite court-ordered injunctions to halt its work, which began following an executive order by President Donald Trump.

The report was released Tuesday morning by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), the ranking member of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

The portal will “almost certainly have significant operating problems” due to rushed development, the whistleblower said. It may lead to failures in the ballot verification process — which under the new system’s “zero percent failure rate” means that if one single ballot’s bar code in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the states.

It could result in millions of voters either receiving their ballots late, or not at all, ahead of the November midterm elections, the whistleblower report said.

The White House and the USPS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the whistleblower report Tuesday.

“We are crossing the Rubicon of American elections,” said Libby Liu, the chief executive officer of Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit legal organization that is representing the whistleblower. “This dangerously defective mail-in ballot process could disenfranchise millions of voters, ensnaring ballots in red tape under the guise of solving a non-existent problem. The whistleblower’s service to our nation is warning the public that their ability to vote is in serious jeopardy.”

This is a developing story and will be updated.

entries.title: CDC Scrubs Two Pennsylvania Measles Deaths From Its Website
entries.summary: The two deaths had been scrutinized by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who suggested they had been wrongly classified or even fabricated.
entries.content:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention removed two measles deaths in Pennsylvania from a national database just days after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly disputed whether state officials had properly classified the cases.

The two deaths had been reflected in the CDC’s national count before being scrubbed over the weekend. The CDC said in a note posted to its website that it was reviewing “additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death.”

Currently available information “does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles,” the note says. The message mirrors the questions raised by Kennedy on Aug. 26 during a public spat with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

Kennedy, a vaccine skeptic who has downplayed the severity of measles outbreaks during his tenure, questioned whether the contagious disease played an active role in the deaths. He also suggested the deaths may have been “fabricated” by one of Shapiro’s staffers.

The fatalities, flagged to the CDC by Pennsylvania on Aug. 25, are the state’s first reported measles-related deaths in 35 years. Pennsylvania has recorded almost 500 measles cases this year, according to the state Department of Health, one of the highest numbers in the country.

One of the two people who died was a newborn who state health officials said had tested positive for measles and died from a ruptured spleen. Both deaths occurred in Pennsylvania’s Lancaster County.

The deaths aggravated Shapiro, who said in a news conference Aug. 26 that there were “real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.”

“Kennedy’s actions to dismantle public health agencies and his language that undermines confidence in vetted medical guidance are contributing to these kinds of outbreaks,” Shapiro wrote on X later in the day. “Just a few years ago, Secretary Kennedy was in Lancaster downplaying the severity of measles and saying that the cure was ‘chicken soup and vitamin A.’”

entries.title: U.S. Strikes Targets in Iran as Hostilities Flare Up Once Again
entries.summary: The conflict had gone more than a month without military action before strikes resumed over the weekend.
entries.content:
By Ben Finley

The U.S. military hit targets in Iran on Tuesday after it said Tehran tried to attack commercial ships and American forces in the Middle East, as hostilities flare once again in an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.

The U.S. strikes, and others on Sunday, abruptly ended a month without military action and threatens to fully reprise a conflict that has spiked global oil prices and posed political problems for Republicans in November's midterm congressional elections. The renewed fighting comes after President Donald Trump appeared to pivot last month toward trying to bend Iran to his will through economic sanctions.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings,” Trump warned on social media after U.S. Central Command announced the latest strikes.

Iranian state TV reported the sound of explosions in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas on Tuesday but did not provide more details.

The U.S. and Iran are both seeking control over the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway off Iran's coast through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows. Tehran’s effectively closed it after the war began.

The Trump administration has argued that striking the right economic target would get Tehran to its breaking point. But at the same time, U.S. stockpiles of advanced weapons have been diminishing, while the war has been unpopular among Americans and could make Republicans vulnerable in November’s midterm elections.

A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted U.S. military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began.

U.S. Central Command said Sunday that its forces struck rocket launchers that would sea mines into the strait, while the U.S. military said Tuesday's strikes were a reaction to attempted attacks on ships in the strait and American forces in the region.

Iran responded to Sunday's attacks by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted, while United Arab Emirates said it stopped an Iranian drone over its waters. President Donald Trump acknowledged Monday that more strikes might be necessary.

The American military in recent days has cast the renewed fighting as limited, though Trump had acknowledged Monday that more strikes might be necessary.

U.S. Central Command said in a statement on X on Monday that its attacks on Iranian targets on Sunday were narrowly focused on preventing Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard forces from placing new mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

“U.S. forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” U.S. Central Command said. “In essence, Iran created the threat and the U.S. military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce.”

Central Command reiterated Tuesday that its attacks followed Iranian aggression against commercial vessels and American troops in the region.

entries.title: U.S. Job Openings Rose Slightly in July
entries.summary: Layoffs fell, but so did the number of people quitting their jobs, according to a Labor Department survey.
entries.content:
By Paul Wiseman

Employers posted slightly more job openings in July but the American labor market remained sturdy in the face of higher costs that are squeezing household budgets.

U.S. job openings ticked up to 7.27 million in July from a revised 7.18 million in June, the Labor Department reported Tuesday.

The department's Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that layoffs fell. But so did the number of people quitting their jobs — a sign of confidence in their prospects. The report showed that gross hiring — before subtracting those who lost or quit their jobs — dipped to 5.1 million in July from 5.3 million in June.

The American job market is hardly booming, but it is ambling along despite an energy shock caused by the fighting with Iran that has squeezed family budgets.

So far this year, U.S. employers — companies, nonprofits and government agencies — added an average of 61,000 net jobs a month. The figure — which was dragged down by job losses in February and July — is unimpressive. But it's an improvement on 2025 when job growth came in below 10,000 a month — weakest hiring outside a recession since 2002 — as the lingering effect of high interest rates and uncertainty caused by Trump's tariffs discouraged firms from hiring.

But if U.S. employers aren't hiring much, at least they aren't firing much either. The unemployment rate remains at a low 4.1%, and the number of people signing up for unemployment benefits has come in low week after week.

“The labor market is back in the ‘low fire, low hire’ mode,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Companies are growing cautious as the war in Iran drags on and borrowing costs have spiked.''

When the Labor Department puts out numbers on August hiring and unemployment Friday, it's expected to show that employers added 65,000 last month and that the jobless rate ticked up to 4.2%, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet.

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Says Mike Rogers Has Been a ‘Beta His Whole Life’
entries.summary: The Michigan Democrat laid out his view of masculinity in an interview with NOTUS.
entries.content:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed accused his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, of compromising his masculinity to appease President Donald Trump, saying in sharply personal terms that the candidate doesn’t know how to be a real man.

“He's been a beta his whole life,” El-Sayed said during an appearance on this week’s On NOTUS. “He's a guy who shows up to laugh extra loud at the alpha’s jokes. And that's what he does with Donald Trump, right? Donald Trump's out here, he says, ‘Mike, jump.’ And Mike says, ‘How high?’”

Rogers, the Democrat added, has “never seen a command from a stronger man that he doesn't want to take.”

https://x.com/NOTUSreports/status/2094818253038096563
El-Sayed faces Rogers in one of the marquee races of the midterm election. Michigan hasn’t elected a Republican senator in more than 30 years but backed Trump in 2024. Republicans have aggressively targeted Michigan after El-Sayed won his party’s competitive primary earlier this month, believing that his unabashedly progressive politics put it in play even amid a difficult political climate for the GOP nationally.

El-Sayed, a former public health official, has sought to portray himself as a progressive champion who can still appeal to young Republican-leaning men, touting his high school football career and love of the University of Michigan’s football team. His campaign against Rogers has increasingly turned into a masculinity contest — last month, he challenged Rogers to a “no pads” face-off on a football field. It’s a theme across Senate races this year: Republican Ken Paxton has suggested his opponent in Texas’ Senate race, Democrat James Talarico, has low testosterone.

In the interview with NOTUS, El-Sayed laid out a conception of masculinity that he set as an alternative to conservative masculinity, including the views articulated by Trump.

“These very small men have tried to make masculinity about punching down. I believe that masculinity is about lifting up, whether you're lifting a weight or you're lifting people around you.”

A Rogers spokesperson dismissed El-Sayed’s criticism.

"While Abdul slings elementary insults, Mike Rogers is focused on fixing our elementary schools,” said Alyssa Brouillet, a Rogers campaign spokesperson. “We have a state to save."

The entire On NOTUS interview with El-Sayed will be released on Wednesday.

entries.title: Milo Yiannopoulos Says He’s ‘Ashamed’ of Supporting Trump After Deportation
entries.summary: The far-right British provocateur had backed Trump’s immigration crackdown before being deported last week.
entries.content:
Far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos is distancing himself from his past support for President Donald Trump after American immigration agents deported him last week.

In an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan that aired Tuesday, Yiannopoulos said his experience being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement had fundamentally changed how he views Trump and the president’s mass-deportation agenda he once aggressively helped promote.

“If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have got involved in supporting Trump in the first place, and I'm very ashamed that I did,” Yiannopoulos said.

Yiannopoulos was deported to the United Kingdom after being detained by ICE in Louisiana. The Department of Homeland Security said he had entered the United States legally in 2019 but overstayed his visa and failed to appear for an immigration hearing. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal in July, and Yiannopoulos told Morgan that the government had canceled his work permit “without telling me” some time in the last year.

“To think that the promise and hope and joy and the anticipation of Trump 2016 could, sort of, over the course of 10 years, collapse into this ugly, warmongering, whole mentally ill heap of crazy — with some of the most unstable and lunatic people, seemingly directing the president's actions,” Yiannopoulos said.

Yiannopoulos rose to prominence as a Breitbart editor and became one of the most recognizable provocateurs associated with the pro-Trump right during the president’s 2016 campaign. He later worked with Kanye West, and helped facilitate a 2022 dinner at Mar-a-Lago attended by Trump, West and far-right political commentator Nick Fuentes.

But Yiannopoulos now says he regrets his support for Trump, coming to that conclusion after experiencing the administration’s immigration enforcement firsthand. He described his recent ICE detention as “brutality” and said he was “swarmed” by 15 agents.

“For the first time, I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified,” he said. “The manner in which they arrest you, they put you in manacles — your hands, your feet — chained together. I mean, everybody who's arrested is like an MS-13 gang member, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like.”

Yiannopoulos’ deportation also intensified a feud with staunch Trump ally Laura Loomer, who said that she repeatedly alerted federal officials about his immigration status.

The Trump administration rejected the idea that Yiannopoulos was targeted for political reasons. Trump border czar Tom Homan said the case was based on Yiannopoulos’ visa overstay, missed immigration hearing and final removal order.

entries.title: Trump Administration Says Chevron Will Expand Venezuela Oil Production
entries.summary: Secretary Chris Wright is traveling to the country days after the White House announced a deal to exert more control over the country’s oil industry.
entries.content:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright is planning to lead a group to Venezuela, as the United States expands its control over the country’s oil industry, a U.S. official told reporters Tuesday.

Wright will be in the country for a forthcoming announcement from Chevron, which plans on increasing its production capacity in Venezuela, the official said. The official spoke under the condition of anonymity under terms set by the White House.

Chevron is the only major U.S. oil company with a presence in Venezuela. Chevron’s expected expansion in the country, and the energy secretary’s visit, come after the White House announced it would be taking control of more than 65 million barrels of oil reserves in Venezuela through an agreement with North American Blue Energy Partners.

Officials provided more details Tuesday on that deal; they said it involved no investment of U.S. dollars – just the country’s backing. The equity position is a “standard deal” similar to others that the Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital has taken in other companies throughout the Trump administration, the officials said.

“Right now, our interest is ensuring that the backing of the U.S. allows this company to attract the investment, the capital investment necessary to ramp up production rapidly,” an official said.

In a fact sheet from the White House released Monday, the Trump administration said the deal will give the U.S. a 35% equity stake in a corporate parent company of North American Blue Energy Partners, a private oil company that now has 100-year concessions for 17 oil fields.

That company will allow the U.S. Department of State to purchase 20% of the oil from those fields, which officials say can go towards refilling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The U.S. will also have the right of first refusal for the other 80% of the company’s production.

The U.S. will have veto power over the North American Blue Energy Partners board of directors.

Officials also addressed the role of Alejandro Betancourt, who runs that company, in the deal. Betancourt was involved in the operation to remove Nicolás Maduro and has worked with the U.S. government since President Donald Trump’s first term. He has also been investigated for money laundering, and senior U.S. officials have helped him avoid criminal charges.

The U.S. government vetted Betancourt, and he is not facing any charges in the United States, an official said Tuesday.

“You have to deal with the dynamics sometimes that are in a place in order to get where you want to get to. This is a proven operator,” the official said. “I’m not nominating anyone for sainthood here. What I am telling you is that this is a person that has, in the past, been helpful to the United States government.”

Though Trump has claimed the deal would lower gas prices, it isn’t expected to have an immediate effect, as many of the oil fields are still undeveloped. Trump met with refining companies and distributors Tuesday to address high gas prices.

Rather, U.S. officials said the Venezuela deal was in the interest of national security, framing it as a “geopolitical opportunity” to secure oil fields previously under the influence of Russian and Chinese companies.

“There is clearly a defined U.S. interest in ensuring one of the largest energy suppliers in our hemisphere is aligned with us, and not with an adversary,” one U.S. official told reporters.

Officials emphasized the U.S.’s desire to see “a stable, democratic Venezuela,” including free and fair elections, and said talks would resume in the middle of September toward that end.

“This is about whether this industry is professionalized, whether it looks like the oil industry of a real country, not a piggy bank for corrupt elements,” the official said. “You don’t want to see the transfer of one kleptocracy to another.”

entries.title: Congress Punts Government Funding Fight Until After the Midterms
entries.summary: A broader budget package is likely to depend on the outcome of the midterm elections.
entries.content:
Congress passed a bipartisan measure to fund federal agencies until mid-December on Tuesday, averting the threat of a government shutdown ahead of the November midterm elections.

The bill advanced through the House 370-48 and will extend current funding levels through Dec. 11. The measure also includes a provision demanded by Democrats that would delay a Trump administration rule putting political appointees in charge of issuing grants.

Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters that the stopgap funding measure was House Republicans’ biggest priority ahead of a scheduled 10-day recess next week.

“We have to make sure the government is funded and we don’t have another Democrat shutdown,” Johnson said before the vote. “I’ll remind y’all they brought about the two longest shutdowns in U.S. history this Congress already, so let’s hope we avoid that.”

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Connecticut), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, told NOTUS that Democrats supported the continuing resolution because it tackled a number of their concerns about border patrol funding, restored funding for some programs that had been previously excluded, and, most notably, the Trump administration grant rule.

Democrats had opposed the initial version of the bill that passed in the House in July.

“If you take a look at what we have accomplished and what's been passed by the Senate and is now here, those things have been addressed,” DeLauro said. “There's no money going to border patrol, the grant rule has been extended through the life of the CR, which gives us time to continue to work on that issue because that has got to get defeated in the long run, and then the anomalies are now included.”

The Senate overwhelmingly approved the funding bill in early August, though that vote was delayed several days over a controversial rule to push back the date that a ban on intoxicating hemp would be implemented.

That provision also saw pushback in the House, where some conservatives called for an immediate ban on the product. Rep. Chip Roy told reporters that he was frustrated by the hemp measure.

“I’m a no on the rule because of that. I’m pretty pissed,” Roy said of the hemp extension. “You’re adding hemp on the back of it, you’re adding CISA on the back of it … there’s like, four, five, six things added on to it.”

Still, the extension of current funding levels gives lawmakers more time to work out a larger government funding deal after those negotiations stalled in July. Lawmakers want to see which party will control each chamber of Congress before determining future funding levels.

But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle seem to be prepared for a bigger fight in December. Republicans are expected to argue to reinstate the Trump administration’s language on grants, which will surely infuriate Democrats and imperil the measure’s passage.

Any struggle over government funding will likely take place in the Senate, where the package needs 60 votes to advance, requiring some bipartisan support. Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told reporters in August that he intends to “fight like hell” to preserve the rule.

DeLauro also said that Democrats are also prepared for a funding showdown over the grant rule.

“There’s got to be a fight about it –– I will initiate a fight about it,” DeLauro said. “It’s the destruction of our system and of the appropriations process.”

entries.title: Bessent Downplays the Bond Market’s Latest Swing: It’s Not ‘Dire’
entries.summary: Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds hit 20-month highs on Tuesday. Economists say reversing the trend will require lowering inflation.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is struggling to assuage investors’ concerns over the U.S. economy.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield hit 4.798% on Tuesday morning, the highest rate for investors’ returns on the government debt in 20 months. The bond market’s new highs cap a summer of volatility for yields that have been climbing since the United States began attacking Iran in February. The stakes are high for the U.S. economy: High bond yields mean higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and consumer credit.

Yields have worsened as investors brace for potential interest rate hikes this month and face uncertainty around President Donald Trump’s inflation-stoking foreign policy and the country’s ballooning debt, economists say.

“Bond yields will keep rising if our fiscal health and inflation concerns aren’t fixed,” Jai Kedia, a research fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, wrote in a text to NOTUS. “If the administration is serious about lowering borrowing costs, it should reverse course on its own bad policies like tariffs and conflict in the Middle East, along with getting government spending back on track.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent downplayed Tuesday’s rising yields in remarks at the Group of 20 summit, a meeting of the world’s top finance ministers taking place in Asheville, North Carolina, this week.

He pointed to the U.S.’s continued economic growth amid the Iran war, including the explosion of the artificial intelligence sector.

“I don’t think that we’re in any kind of a dire situation,” Bessent said during a discussion with Fox Business host Larry Kudlow. “The U.S. bond market has been the best-performing bond market. What happens over a month doesn’t matter.”

The administration has been sensitive to the bond market’s swings, however. Bessent attempted to soothe concerns in August, announcing an initiative to offload at least $4 billion in government debt from the market. Bond yields quickly rebounded, however, and have remained high.

Inflation is currently a primary driver of bond yields, economists told NOTUS. Investors have been in limbo this year as the Federal Reserve has punted on interest rate changes. There are some signs investors anticipate interest rates will go up to tamp down inflation, especially after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh noted the issue in his first major speech at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last week.

“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” Warsh said. “Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job, that’s our mandate and that’s our charge to keep.”

Economists say the only lasting way out of the bond yield problem is to tackle inflation and the economy’s structural issues. Conservatives have pointed to the federal deficit, calling to reduce government spending — something Bessent also alluded to last month.

“The No. 1 thing the U.S. government can do to reduce those yields is to reduce the deficit,” said Judge Glock, the research director at the conservative Manhattan Institute. “It would also assure bondholders and bond traders that the U.S. could get its debt under control over the long term.”

Ryan Young, a senior economist with the libertarian Competitive Enterprise Institute, noted that Tuesday’s yield highs could also be the result of the news cycle, including Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech, flaring tensions between the U.S. and Canada and resumed fighting in Iran.

“What’s happening today could well get canceled out tomorrow, but in the long-run trajectory until something does get done about the debt situation, I would look for a slow long-term creep-up, along with plenty of day-to-day volatility as stories pop up,” Young said.

Conservative economists are skeptical the Treasury can influence bond yields through its buyback operation. Glock said the Treasury can’t lay down those billions of dollars in funds without eventually recouping them through additional debt.

“There’s fundamentally no way that buyback program can work over the medium or long term,” he said. “It’s effectively trading one form of debt for another.”

entries.title: Trump Nominates Hung Cao for Navy Secretary
entries.summary: Cao was elevated to acting secretary in April when John Phelan abruptly resigned.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he plans to nominate acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to hold the post permanently.

"The Senate needs to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP, so he ‌can ⁠continue the fantastic work he has been doing over ⁠the past 4 months," Trump wrote ⁠in a Truth Social post Tuesday.

Cao was elevated to acting secretary in April when John Phelan abruptly stepped down.

The Pentagon has seen a number of high-profile departures and removals during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s tenure. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation on Monday and is expected to leave the role in the coming days.

entries.title: Florida Becomes First State to Remove Flock Cameras From State Roads
entries.summary: Florida’s decision came days after Gov. Ron DeSantis raised concerns about the technology.
entries.content:
Florida is ordering law-enforcement agencies to remove automated license-plate readers from state roads, becoming the first in the country to remove existing Flock cameras from state-controlled highways.

On Monday, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license-plate readers on state roads, giving agencies 30 days to remove them before the state takes them down. The department also said it will no longer approve permits for new readers.

The move reflects a growing public backlash against the technology company Flock Safety, whose cameras are used by law enforcement nationwide to track vehicles and aid investigations.

The Florida Department of Transportation cited the rapid growth of the technology and concerns about its use.

“While Florida law limits the issuance of permits for LPR systems to law enforcement agencies, the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life,” The department’s chief operating officer, Will Watts, wrote in a memo.

The directive applies to cameras installed within the rights-of-way of the state highway system. It does not prohibit cameras installed on private property, including commercial developments, and does not automatically eliminate cameras on roads controlled by cities and counties.

While Florida is the first state to revoke camera permits and remove existing readers from state roads, other states and local governments began restricting the technology in a bipartisan wave this year. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered all state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras, while Washington state implemented tighter regulations on data sharing and handling. A number of candidates in local and national races from both parties have also criticized the devices or called for their elimination.

Florida’s decision came days after Gov. Ron DeSantis raised concerns about the technology, even as he defended its usefulness to law enforcement.

“I’m all about having law enforcement have tools to be able to hold criminals accountable,” the Republican governor said at Florida International University last week. “But I don’t want to have this become a surveillance state.”

DeSantis has also pointed to recent examples of alleged misuse of the technology by law-enforcement officers. In one Florida case, an officer was accused of using license-plate-reader data to track an ex-girlfriend.

Some Florida law-enforcement agencies say they are now working to remove the cameras. The Putnam County sheriff's office said it would discontinue its Flock program, while other agencies affirmed they would comply with the state's 30-day deadline.
