entries.title: DOJ Leader Encourages Employees to Sign Up for Election Monitor Duty
entries.summary: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon has said she hopes to dispatch 1,000 monitors nationwide on Election Day.
entries.content:
The head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division on Tuesday urged attorneys and staffers under her supervision to sign up as election monitors, in what appears to be part of a plan to deploy 1,000 monitors to polls in November.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, in an email to Civil Rights Division employees reviewed by NOTUS, said she was seeking attorneys and professional staff to fan out to an unspecified number of polling places around the country on Nov. 3 or work a call center in Washington.

The Justice Department has long sent federal election monitors to watch voting during primaries, midterms and presidential elections, and it’s typical for such internal recruitment memos to go out at this point in the election cycle.

But Dhillon’s note carries a heightened significance in light of her move to send an unprecedented number of monitors to polls.

Dhillon told Bloomberg in an interview published Aug. 17 that the 1,000 monitors she hopes to dispatch would watch for compliance with voting accessibility rules and other civil rights issues within the Civil Rights Division’s purview — in addition to cases of election fraud, which has not historically been the division’s mandate.

She made no mention of those instructions in her email to staff Tuesday, saying only that the division “has the opportunity and obligation to ensure the upcoming midterm elections are free and fair.”

“As in prior elections,” she wrote, “our nationwide monitoring of the voting process on Election Day is essential to ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.”

She added a bolded call to action: “I’m writing to encourage each of you to sign up and join us in this effort.”

According to the email, those who sign up for election monitoring will be required to complete two short training sessions ahead of time, which has been customary for election monitors. Those who sign up for the Election Day call center must complete at least one training session. Monitors will receive their location assignments “a few weeks before the election,” the email said.

Anna Baldwin, a former attorney in the division’s Voting Section, who frequently deployed to serve in election monitoring roles, said the agency has always prioritized the assignments to voting locations. Those efforts focused on mundane oversight, such as whether locations were providing bilingual services when required to do so.

The DOJ’s monitors historically have spoken to voters who have left the polling stations to identify problem areas that could be addressed after Election Day, she said.

“There would not be this free-floating search for fraud that Harmeet Dhillon is citing for sending out this exaggeratedly large number of monitors,” Baldwin said.

A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment, saying the department doesn’t confirm or discuss internal emails.

Other former Civil Rights Division officials questioned how the office would manage to recruit and train anywhere near 1,000 monitors in time to be sent to the field for Election Day.

The division’s staff has diminished significantly on Dhillon’s watch through firings and resignations. And nearly all of the roughly three-dozen attorneys and managers who served in the Voting Section prior to Trump’s second term have departed, draining the unit of important institutional knowledge, according to former officials.

“I worry about who will lead these teams and who will run these exercises, and what kind of experience and training they have,” said a former Civil Rights Division official who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Across the division, NOTUS previously reported, a majority of current attorneys were hired since Trump took office last year. Many have ties to conservative organizations and offices, and some have a history of engaging in failed efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election.

If the DOJ sends out 1,000 monitors, former staff said some of that total would have to come from outside of the Civil Rights Division. Such an approach would be highly unusual, as the department has always preferred to limit its deployments to those with expertise in voting and civil rights law.

In response to a previous inquiry from NOTUS, the Justice Department said in an emailed statement that all election monitors would be drawn from within the federal government, but did not specify where. Officials are not recruiting from outside private groups, the department said.

About 700 monitors went out during the 2024 presidential election, when millions more Americans voted than are expected in the midterm elections, according to former officials. Most were from the Justice Department, while a smaller portion came from an Office of Personnel Management program that hires election observers to watch specific voting locations that are under consent decrees, settlements, or other court orders. In 2022, the previous midterm election cycle, about 280 monitors were dispatched to polls.

Employees can volunteer to either physically deploy to polling locations or work at an Election Day call center. In the former option, they will find out their location a few weeks before Nov. 3. In either case, they will retain their normal pay. 

Dhillon’s monitor initiative comes amid a broader attempt by the Trump administration to crack down on what officials have referred to as widespread fraud in election administration and possible noncitizen voting, which experts say is extremely rare.

Under Dhillon, the Civil Rights Division has sued dozens of states that refused her requests to turn over full, unredacted copies of their voter registration data. So far, federal judges have ruled against the department in 23 of those cases and ruled in the government’s favor in none, according to tracking by the University of Wisconsin.

Some state and local officials, as well as outside election advocates, have raised concerns about the potential for a large volume of monitors to disrupt election administration or interfere with poll workers and voters, particularly if they receive instructions to investigate alleged fraud or other issues.

Just last week, Wyoming’s Republican governor asked the state’s attorney general to look into what he called “aggressive” behavior from DOJ monitors during the state’s primary. Debra Lee, the county clerk of Laramie County, told local media that two monitors had asked how the county acquired its election equipment, inquired about poll worker training and sought to examine tabulators. She said they also did not present their credentials until she asked for them and planned to interview voters at the polling place, which the county doesn’t allow.

The solicitation for election monitors has always been voluntary, former attorneys in the division said, though they added that current staff are likely to interpret the call differently after Dhillon has employed aggressive tactics of reassigning staff and firing career employees. Despite the pressure, there does not appear to be immediate enthusiasm for the assignments.

“No one I know wants to sign up for it,” said a current division attorney, who was granted anonymity out of fear of retaliation.

While Dhillon told employees they would go through two training sessions if selected for the deployments, the makeover of the division has created some concern about what those will now entail. The official who led those trainings for the last two decades joined the max exodus of staff under Trump.

In her interview last month with Bloomberg, Dhillon said monitors would be trained on the same materials used in previous administrations. Even if that’s the case, however, a different crop of Voting Section attorneys may be overseeing those who sign up to visit poll sites.

Former officials said that could create inconsistencies in what they look for and how they conduct themselves with election officials, poll workers and voters.

“I think we’re just going to see a broad range of behaviors,” a former Voting Section attorney said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. “If it’s just two trainings and everyone’s pretty much new, people will have to resort to their own instincts in the field.”

entries.title: A Convicted Elections Clerk Turned Down a California Job After Newsom Stepped In
entries.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom said “election deniers not welcome here” before Tina Peters declined the post in Shasta County.
entries.content:
Tina Peters, a former Colorado elections clerk convicted for tampering in the 2020 presidential election, was reportedly set to take a job overseeing the November election for a conservative northern California county — until Gov. Gavin Newsom piped up.

“A convicted MAGA election tamperer working in an elections office,” the California governor wrote Monday on X. “What could possibly go wrong? TINA, NOT IN CALIFORNIA! ELECTION DENIER FELONS NOT WELCOME HERE!!!”

By Tuesday morning, Peters had turned down the job offer, Shasta County registrar of voters Clint Curtis told the Los Angeles Times. Curtis said Peters declined the offer “because she’s running around the country right now trying to secure the elections.”

“Shasta County lost out,” Curtis added.

Peters was sentenced to nine years in a Colorado prison for orchestrating a security breach of county election equipment but was released in June after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, commuted her sentence under pressure from President Donald Trump.

Trump had threatened to take harsh measures if Peters was not released, citing her declining health and perpetuating the false claim that she discovered a Democrat-led plot to steal the 2020 presidential election.

entries.title: House Votes to Censure Chuck Edwards Over Harassment Allegations
entries.summary: The North Carolina Republican ended his reelection bid following mounting pressure from his party.
entries.content:
The House voted to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards on Tuesday following a House Ethics Committee report that determined there was “substantial evidence” that the North Carolina Republican engaged in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young staffers.”

The measure passed 413-2, with Edwards and another Republican voting against censure. The Ethics Committee recommended the move after its investigation this year concluded that “there was substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.”

“The Committee therefore has recommended that the House of Representatives adopt the Report, and with it, a censure of Representative Edwards for the conduct described therein,” the committee wrote in an August press release.

The resulting scandal led Edwards to end his reelection bid earlier this year following mounting pressure from House Republicans.

Tuesday’s measure does not strip Edwards of his committee assignments or restrict his voting abilities, but is the highest form of discipline a member can receive short of expulsion. It requires Edwards to stand in the chamber as the resolution condemning his behavior is read aloud.

Edwards spoke on the House floor shortly before the vote, apologizing to the two female staffers at the center of the allegations as well as his wife and family.

“Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment,” Edwards said. “I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret the discomfort that some of my actions may have caused and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode, while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence just simply does not support.”

Edwards has maintained that he did not engage in sexual misconduct, sending lawmakers a 22-page letter defending his actions last week. In the letter, the Republican said that there is “no House rule prohibiting members and staff from being friends.”

Edwards told reporters ahead of the censure vote on Tuesday that “House members should look closely at the process and how the Ethics Committee has chosen to abandon its own rules and make up the rules as they go.”

Sources told NOTUS in May that the committee had launched an investigation into allegations that Edwards had an affair with his former deputy chief of staff, who left his office earlier this year.

Multiple sources told NOTUS that Edwards and the former deputy chief of staff were not entirely private and the relationship became well-known among staff. The rules of the House of Representatives prohibit members from having romantic or sexual relationships with employees under their supervision.

The committee’s report found that Edwards was aware his conduct toward staffers had generated “rumors” and lists instances of alleged inappropriate conduct with staffers. The report found that Edwards went beyond the norms of professional behavior by giving two staffers “lavish gifts.”

“Both women received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners,” the report said.

Lawmakers have employed censures more frequently to target their rivals in recent years, though most recent votes have largely fallen along partisan lines. Edwards was the first Republican to be censured under GOP leadership in decades.

The case is also one in a series of recent high-profile incidents involving lawmakers and staffers. Former Reps. Eric Swalwell of California and Tony Gonzales of Texas both resigned after ethics investigations into sexual misconduct allegations.

NOTUS reported that the Ethics Committee also investigated another North Carolina member, Rep. Alma Adams, for an inappropriate relationship with a staffer. Adams' office said the panel did not find an improper relationship.
entries.author: Avani Kalra

entries.title: House Republicans Pass Resolution Denouncing Socialism
entries.summary: The measure also includes a call to enact the SAVE America Act, a provision one Democrat called a “poison pill.”
entries.content:
The House passed a resolution Tuesday to “condemn and denounce” socialism and the policy positions of the Democratic Socialists of America, a key messaging vote for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The measure was approved 220-192 with eight Democrats voting in favor. Two Democrats voted "present."

The resolution also includes a call for the “enactment” of a voter-ID bill that President Donald Trump has repeatedly called his top policy priority. Democrats have panned the SAVE America Act, which requires proof of citizenship for voter registration and restricts mail-in ballots, saying it will prevent eligible voters from exercising their rights.

Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday that the extent to which lawmakers align with socialist ideas is a major point of concern for voters around the country this year.

“The question that voters across the nation have to answer this fall is whether we’re going to turn the greatest nation in the history of the world over to communism and state government socialism,” Johnson said.

Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colorado), who introduced the resolution, said in a statement that the rise in the number of DSA-affiliated Democrats expected to come to Congress in January was a motivating factor.

“Socialism is fundamentally at odds with our values as Americans,” Crank said. “American citizens being able to securely cast their votes at the ballot box is a right that the Democratic Socialists of America are actively working to undermine.”

But some centrist Democrats said the measure is “not serious” and was solely designed for Republicans to discuss on the campaign trail.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Florida) said more Democrats would have voted in favor if the SAVE America component was not included and accused Republicans of attaching the provision on purpose, in order to attack Democrats on the campaign trail for voting against the resolution.

“It’s a poison pill,” Moskowitz said before the vote. “They’re trying to jam Democrats, get us to vote against socialism. They’re trying to jam me and 20 others that are running in these toss-up seats to try to vote to support socialism by voting against the resolution.”

Moskowitz, alongside Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-New Jersey), Hillary Scholten (D-Michigan) and Tom Suozzi (D-New York) introduced an amendment on Monday to strip the voter-ID-bill language out of the proposed resolution.

Moskowitz said he helped author the amendment in order to call Republicans’ bluff, adding that if GOP leadership was serious about the provision it would accept the proposed amendment.

“They’re not going to, because it’s all politics. That’s the whole point,” Moskowitz said. “They want to use this as a politicization as we go into the election.”

entries.title: New Emails Show Greg Bovino Was Under Investigation Prior to His Retirement
entries.summary: Former Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino denied allegations of misconduct and said the investigation forced him into retirement.
entries.content:
Former senior Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino faced an internal investigation prior to his retirement over his lack of credibility and for making offensive remarks about a federal prosecutor’s Jewish faith, according to public records released by Customs and Border Protection.

The emails, which were released in response to Freedom of Information Act litigation, showed CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility contacted Bovino on March 2 for an official inquiry. The office asked him to answer a series of questions in a declaration, including those related to an incident where Bovino allegedly mocked a U.S. attorney for observing the Sabbath, asking, "Do Orthodox criminals also take off Saturday?"

That attorney, a Minnesota federal prosecutor, was not identified in the records, but The New York Times and CBS News reported in June that Bovino was referring to Daniel Rosen, who is an Orthodox Jew.

Bovino was alleged to have said the comments at the height of his authority as “Border Patrol commander-at-large,” a position that made him the face for the Trump administration’s immigration-enforcement operations. He was demoted in January after federal immigration officers fatally shot U.S. citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and announced his retirement in a Breitbart interview published March 16. Bovino has since been critical of Trump administration officials, including White House border czar Tom Homan.

The declaration also asked Bovino to respond to U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis’ findings that he lied during sworn testimonies in a deposition that spanned late October and early November 2025 concerning his use of crowd-control tactics in Chicago.

Bovino did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the internal investigation Tuesday.

He denied allegations of misconduct in a statement Tuesday to Border Hawk, a far-right news outlet. Bovino said he was forced into retirement when CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott “weaponized” the Office of Professional Responsibility against him, saying Scott viewed Bovino as his “de facto political rival.”

Bovino told the outlet he was unaware that he was under investigation until a Times reporter called him in March. He said OPR had no “witnesses or testimony” and that he had “enough experience to know I wouldn’t get a fair shake” from the investigation. He said he was advised by his attorneys to retire immediately.

Bovino said two OPR agents appeared at his home without a warrant in March, and he retired the following day.

The Department of Homeland Security “does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency,” a spokesperson said in a statement Tuesday.

entries.title: Media Site Asks Judge to Block Trump From Posting Official News on Truth Social
entries.summary: The Intercept’s chief executive said, “The First Amendment doesn’t have a paywall.”
entries.content:
A left-leaning news organization asked a federal judge on Tuesday to bar President Donald Trump and his close associates from posting official government announcements on Truth Social as long as it’s selling faster access to the president’s market-moving social feed.

The Intercept, in a suit filed in New York, is seeking an injunction against such posts and asking a judge to declare the move to sell access “unconstitutional and unlawful.”

Last month, Truth Social began charging users up to $100,000 a month for “Truth API,” a feature granting corporate clients and high-frequency trading firms a first look at the president’s posts. The Intercept and co-plaintiff Freedom of the Press Foundation originally sued the president on Aug. 12, arguing het is trading Americans’ First Amendment rights for profit.

“Trump doesn’t get to charge people for his own public statements,” Annie Chabel, The Intercept’s chief executive, said in a Tuesday news release. “The First Amendment doesn’t have a paywall, and we’re not going to let him build one.”

The plaintiffs are also seeking a preliminary injunction to prohibit Trump’s executive assistant Natalie Harp and his deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino from posting White House announcements “so long as 'Truth API' is in operation."

The two are believed to be the only aides with access to the president’s Truth Social account.

In an earnings call last month, Trump Media’s interim CEO Kevin McGurn told investors that clients had already begun buying access to the president’s social feed.

And while the White House has not publicly commented on the suit, McGurn characterized Trump API as perfectly legal.

“Providing licensed real-time public data through commercial APIs is a well-established business practice across the technology, financial information and media industries,” McGurn said on the earnings call. “This is no different.”

Trump created Truth Social in 2021 after he was removed from Twitter, and he remains the largest shareholder in its parent company, Trump Media. According to the court filings, the plaintiffs claim the president and top aides “frequently and exclusively” use the platform to declare military attacks, fire agency heads and announce major domestic policies — communications that frequently rouse market rallies.
